<reason>Both sides quickly converged on proportionality, so the debate reduced to whether the proportional pathway must be a technique-keyed route "distinct from traditional GMO regulation" (as the motion says) or a unified product-based tiering system (CON's counterproposal). CON won that narrowed clash. Its strongest move was to take PRO's own concrete eligibility test (functional knowledge of the allele, comparative composition, agronomic data, no safety-relevant departure) and show every criterion is a product criterion — so "distinct" does no safety work and functions as a privilege attached to a tool, with a gaming boundary. PRO's reply that "its administrative boundary need not be its safety rationale" largely concedes the point and leaves PRO holding only an administrative-feasibility/speed benefit, which CON then shrank with a sharp squeeze: a pathway limited to alleles already cultivated and eaten buys crossing speed, not capability, while the disease-resistance and drought benefits PRO opened with fall into full assessment. That "safe version is nearly empty, useful version is the one my potato/cassava cases break" dilemma was never squarely answered. PRO argued well and honestly: its parity counter-question (CON's own tiers require the same screening, so either evidence can justify different workloads or CON collapses too) forced CON's best clarification, and its duplication-vs-threshold distinction plus the point that keeping GMO rules does not make breeding history detectable partly defuse the detection asymmetry. But PRO's concession that a rejected shipment "can indeed hurt the farmer" handed CON a memorable weighing line, and PRO never developed the strongest defense of its feasibility claim beyond assertion. CON's two clipped speeches are a real execution cost, and its "fast lanes always widen" mechanism stayed largely assertive, which keeps the margin from being large.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 answer to Q1: reframing PRO's eligibility criteria as entirely product-based, so that "distinct" is a label rather than a safety rationale, combined with the undetectability asymmetry (lightest review for products no port assay, recall, or shopper can ever identify). PRO's "administrative boundary need not be its safety rationale" reply conceded the frame rather than breaking it.</best_rebuttal>
